ངོ་བོ་ནི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེ་ན། མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། མཐོང་བའི་ཡུལ་ཡང་དེ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །བྱ་བ་ལས་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ལྟ་ཡིན་ན་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་བྱེད་པ་པོར་གྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་གཅིག་པ་ཅན་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་གསལ་བར་བྱས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
གཅིག་དངོས་གཅིག་གི་རྣམ་པ་ཞེས། །དབང་ཕྱུག་གིས་ནི་བསྟན་པ་མིན། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཚད་མས་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གཉི་ག་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེ་ན། མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རང་དབང་དུ་མི་རྟོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །རྒྱབ་རྟེན་གང་གིས་མཐོང་བ་གནོད་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན། རེ་ཞིག་དོན་
ནི་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བག་ཆགས་ཀྱང་གཉི་ག་ལ་མཚུངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མཐོང་བས་རང་གི་ཡུལ་ལ་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པར་བྱེད་ན་བཟློག་པ་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། མ་གསལ་བ་ཡིན་ན་རྣམ་པར་འཇོག་པ་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །མཐོང་བས་ངོ་བོ་གཞན་མ་མཐོང་བ་ཉིད་ནི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པའི་ཡུལ་ཡིན་
གྱི། རང་དབང་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ཉིད་ནི་ངོ་བོ་གཞན་ལ་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ངོ་བོ་གཉིས་ཕན་ཚུན་རྗེས་སུ་འཇུག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པས་གཅིག་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེས་རྟོགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་རང་དབང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གནོད་བྱ་ཉིད་ཡིན་ནོ། །རྣམ་པར་བརྟག་བྱའི་བཟློག་པ་ནི་མཐོང་བ་
ལས་གཞན་པ་ཉིད་དུ་རྟོགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །མཐོང་བའི་བྱ་བའི་རྗེས་སུ་འཇུག་པ་ཅན་ནི་སྔོན་པོའི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་ལས་ཡིན་པ་བཞིན་དུ། དེ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྤངས་ནས་འཇུག་པ་ནི་འགལ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ནི་ཐོག་མ་མེད་པའི་བག་ཆགས་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་
པར་རྟོག་པས་ཕྱི་རོལ་ཉིད་དུ་སྒྲོ་བཏགས་པ་ན་མཐོང་བ་ན་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་ཟེར་བ་ནི། བྱེ་བྲག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དམིགས་པར་བྱ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིར་སྨྲས་པ། དེ་ནི་རྟོགས་བྱེད་བརྗོད་བྱ་ཉིད། །ཚད་མ་པ་ལ་རིགས་མ་ཡིན། །ཚད་མ་ལ་ལྟོས་མི་དེ་ཉིད། །དེ་ལ་ལྟོས་
པ་མེད་པར་གནས། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ཡོངས་སུ་རྟོགས་པར་བྱེད་པའི་སློབ་མ་རྣམས་ལ་གཏན་ཚིགས་ཀྱིས་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །བློ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཉེ་བར་དམིགས་པ་ནི་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་བཞིན་དུ་འཇུག་པར་བྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་སུམ་དང་འགལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་ནི་བསྒྲུབ་བྱ་ལ་

If one argues that the essential nature is understood by conceptual thought itself, it is not so, because the object of direct perception is the opposite of that. If one argues that it is understood through action, then if that were the case, because conceptual thought would be the agent, it would clearly establish a great unity <note>the author is refuting the idea of a singular, permanent creative agent or a unified conceptual subject</note>.

It is said:
The form of a single entity
Was not shown by the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> <gloss>The Supreme Lord or Creator in Hindu philosophy</gloss>.

This is not the case because it is established by valid cognition <term>pramana</term>. If one argues that both are knowledge, it is not so, because they are not understood independently. What support could invalidate what is seen by direct perception? For a moment, the object does not exist, and the habitual tendencies <term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious imprints or predispositions</gloss> are equal for both.

If direct perception establishes its own object, it does so by clearing away its opposite. If the object is not clear, there is no establishment. The fact that direct perception does not see another essence is the object of conceptual thought, but it is not independent, because that very thing causes one to understand another essence. It is not so: because the two essences do not follow one another, they are not one. Therefore, what is called understanding by that is not independent and is thus subject to being invalidated.

The opposite of what is to be conceptualized does not occur because it is not understood as something other than what is seen. Just as the following of the activity of seeing arises from the conceptualization of blue, it is not contradictory to engage after having thoroughly abandoned what is not that <note>the process of excluding what an object is not, known as apoha</note>.

When that very thing is superimposed as being external by conceptual thought arising from beginningless habitual tendencies, to say it does not exist when seen is not something to be perceived by those such as the <term>Vaisheshika</term> <gloss>an ancient school of Indian philosophy emphasizing atomism and logic</gloss> who have not thoroughly established the distinctions.

Here it is said:
That which is the means of understanding and the subject of expression
Is not appropriate for a follower of valid cognition.
That which does not depend on valid cognition
Exists without depending on it.

This is shown by logical reason to the students who are seeking to thoroughly understand. Engaging in observation based on the mind does not function like a proof, because it contradicts direct perception. By the proof, the thing to be proven <unclear>one line of text regarding the relationship between proof and the proven</unclear>

<summary>This page analyzes the relationship between direct perception and conceptual thought, refuting the idea that conceptual thought independently establishes reality. It discusses the Buddhist logical theory of exclusion and challenges Vaisheshika views on external existence.</summary>
<keywords>direct perception, conceptual thought, valid cognition, Ishvara, Vaisheshika, habitual tendencies, exclusion, proof</keywords>

པའི་ཕྱིར་མིང་གཞན་འཇུག་པར་མི་རིགས་སོ། །འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མྱུར་དུ་གོ་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཕམ་པའི་གཞི་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་གཞན་ལ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་ལ་སྒྲའི་དབང་ཉིད་དུ་ཐེ་ཚོམ་དུ་གྱུར་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། བསྒྲུབ་བྱ་ལ་
ཡང་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་ཟེར་བ་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། དོན་ལ་སྟེ། དབྱིབས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་དཔྱད་པ་ནི། བུམ་པ་དང་ས་གཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་ཐ་དད་པར་རོ། །དངོས་པོའི་འཁྲུལ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། དངོས་པོ་ནི་དོན་དེའིའོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སྒྲ་གཅིག་གི་
ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་དག་གིས་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་གཅིག་གི་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་དག་གི་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བཀག་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་དག་གིས་བསྒྲུབ་བྱ་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་ལྡོག་པར་རྟོགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དབྱིབས་ཀྱི་ཙམ་ནི་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་མ་
ཡིན་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ལ་སྒྲུབ་(བྱད་,བྱེད་)གཅིག་ཉིད་ཅེས་པ་ལྟོས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སྒྲ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་མི་འབྱུང་ལ་མེད་ཀྱང་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར། སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་ནི་དེའི་དབང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་ཟེར་བས་བསྒྲུབ་བྱ་ནི་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་མེད་ན་སྒྲ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་མི་འགྲུབ་པ་ལ། དེ་མེད་ཀྱང་སྒྲུབ་བྱེད་ཡོད་ན་འགྲུབ་པ་
ཡིན་པས་དེའི་དབང་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་གང་ལ་ཡང་སྒྲ་རྟག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གཞལ་བྱ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མི་རྟག་པ་ཡང་ཡིན་ཏེ། མིག་གིས་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་གཞལ་བྱ་ཉིད་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྒྲ་ནི་རང་གི་

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>Therefore, it is incorrect to apply a different name. Because this very point is understood quickly, it constitutes the ultimate ground of defeat; this is because there is no other reason.

Regarding the claim that just as the nature of the word itself is doubtful as a proof, the same applies to the probandum <note>original: "bsgrub bya"; the thesis or subject to be proven</note>, if one asks "how," it means: in reality. The investigation based on shape and so on differs regarding the pot, the ground, and such things. The phrase "error regarding the entity" refers to the entity of that specific object.

Similarly, by means of two verses, the presence and absence of a single word is refuted by the presence and absence of a single proof <note>original: "sgrub byed"; the logical reason or evidence</note>. The presence and absence of the probandum is not determined by the presence and absence of that <note>the word</note>, because no such reverse relation <note>original: "ldog pa"; the logical contrapositive where the absence of the result implies the absence of the cause</note> is perceived.

The statement "mere shape is not the proof" depends on the idea of a "single proof." Similarly, because the result does not occur even if the word is present, and does occur even if it is absent, it is said that the proof is not dependent on the word. It will be shown that the probandum is dependent on the proof because it is not established if the proof is absent even if the word is present, yet it is established if the proof is present even if the word is absent.

Therefore, in examples such as "sound is permanent because it is an object of knowledge" or "it is impermanent because it is visible to the eye," words like "object of knowledge" establish their own referents. In these cases, one <note>the reason</note> is not mistaken regarding the property to be proven. However, because the proof in these instances is mistaken or unestablished, the probandum does not fall under its power. For that very reason, they are faulty.

To show that a lack of quality is not caused by the quality of the word, it is said: "If that itself is mistaken and so on." A quality is a quality only by virtue of the quality of the proof; a fault is not caused by the fault of the word. As it has been said: "Even if the word is not established, the entity is..." Similarly, that itself is the fault because of the fault in the proof; at that time, even if it possesses qualities...

<summary>This page discusses the logical relationship between words, proofs, and the subjects being proven, arguing that the validity of an argument depends on the evidence rather than the terminology used. It clarifies that logical faults arise from the proof's failure to establish the thesis, not from the linguistic properties of the words themselves.</summary>
<keywords>logic, proof, probandum, error, presence and absence, Tibetan Buddhist epistemology, Pramana</keywords>

It is shown that subsequent realization arises from conceptualizations such as activity and the like, but not from attachment and the like. Regarding the statement, "If one engages in conventional expression," the connection to the latter half is that it is an <term>upalepa</term> <gloss>affliction or staining</gloss>, as stated below. Great peace is <term>nirvana</term> <gloss>liberation from suffering</gloss>.

To show that following attachment is disparaged even in the context of visible phenomena, it is said that it is "afflicted by attachment and the like." One investigates the next world based on conceptualization. Regarding the objects of that world, such as the apprehended, the apprehender, the composite whole, the self, and the possessions of the self, one might think that while the next world is established, the establishment of enemies and such would not occur. To address this, it is stated that "conceptualization which follows what is seen" is the sign of conventional expression, while the other is not. Therefore, to show the purpose of following what is seen—namely that it does not turn away from non-duality and the like—it says "if certain." In the <term>Vijnaptimatra</term> <gloss>Mind-Only</gloss> school, the eyes and other faculties are like a dream; they are untrue through mere manifestation. However, that which is non-deceptive in functional utility is true because it is distinguished by a specific cultivation. Even if consciousness alone were external, it would arise as mere desire because it is produced by cultivation. To conclude that the next world exists just like consciousness itself, despite being dissimilar in definition from other external things, it asks, "Are the eyes and so forth truly real?"

If one realizes unseen distinctions from seeing distinct results, then it is unreasonable to say that only what is seen by the potent is the object of analysis for cultivation. One might think this is because distinctions in the elements, such as solidity and the like, are seen. Regarding the thought, "If there is a distinction of the great elements," the answer is: "Where heat, moisture, and so forth are born." <summary>This page discusses the Buddhist epistemological view on how conceptualization and cultivation lead to the realization of truth, contrasting the Mind-Only perspective on reality with conventional experience. It explores the relationship between sensory faculties, the elements, and the continuity of the mind into the next life.</summary>

ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པ་ནི། ཡོད་མིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ། མངོན་སུམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གནས་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུའོ། །ཁྱེད་ཅག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་འཁོར་བ་པའོ། །འཁྲུལ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། མངོན་སུམ་མ་ཡིན་པའོ། །
བདག་ལ་གནོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་ལ་རྒྱབ་ཀྱིས་ཕྱོགས་པ་ནི་ཞེ་སྡང་ཡིན་པ་ལ་བདག་དང་བདག་གིར་ལྟ་བའི་སྙིང་པོ་ཅན་གྱིས་རྒྱབ་ཀྱིས་ཕྱོགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་། །ཕྱོགས་པ་ཙམ་ཡོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་ཟེར་བ་ལ་བསྟན་པ་ནི། མི་གཙང་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མཐོང་བ་ལས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རང་
བཞིན་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་ཡུལ་གཅིག་ལ་ཀུན་དུ་སྦྱོར་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདི་ལ་ཡང་། བྱམས་སོགས་རྨོངས་དང་འགལ་མེད་ཕྱིར། །ཤིན་ཏུ་ཉེས་པ་ཚར་གཅོད་མིན། །ཞེས་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ལན་བསྟན་པ་ནི། མི་སྡུག་པ་བསྒོམ་པས་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །མི་རྟག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པར་
ལྟ་བ་ལ་ཡང་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞེས་ཟེར་བ་ལ། བདག་ཡོད་ན་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །མི་རྟག་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ལྟ་བར་འཁྲུལ་པ་དང་འགལ་བར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། གང་གི་ཚེ་རྒྱུ་ལ་རག་ལས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བ་རྣམས་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་ལྟ་བ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། བདག་ཏུ་ལྟ་བའི་སྙིང་
པོ་ཅན་གྱི་ཞེ་སྡང་མི་སྲིད་དེ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་རྣམས་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཅན་ཡིན་གྱི་སྙིང་རྗེ་མ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། གཏི་མུག་ཉེས་པའི་རྩ་བ་སྟེ། ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ཉེས་རྒྱུ་ལ་ནི་གནོད་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལའོ། །ཉེས་མེད་ནི་ཉེས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བའི

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Buddhist logic and epistemology, specifically addressing the relationship between the concept of self, compassion, and the elimination of afflictive emotions like hatred.</meta>

The thought that "it is only thus" is expressed by the phrase: *if it is mine*. If happiness were to reside in a self, it is shown that one would certainly superimpose the idea of a self; this is expressed by the phrase: *if it were for the sake of a self*. If it resides in another, how could it be a superimposition of a self? This is shown by the phrase: *merely for the sake of another*. 

In response to the objection, "How can it not be of great purpose?" the *example of the king* is given. This means that it is an engagement for the sake of others. To show that even one who is free from conceptual construction <term>vikalpa</term> <gloss>mental activity that categorizes and labels experience</gloss> engages through the force of previous deeds, the phrase: *from the preceding and preceding* is used. 

To clarify that very point, the phrase: *it is not existent* is used, because it is not an object of direct perception <term>pratyakṣa</term> <gloss>immediate, non-conceptual cognition</gloss>. *Not abiding* refers to the state of emptiness regarding the welfare of sentient beings. The term *you all* refers to those in cyclic existence <term>saṃsāra</term> <gloss>the continuous cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</gloss>. The term *error* refers exclusively to conceptual construction; it is not direct perception.

Regarding the objection that turning away from what harms the self is hatred, and although it is not necessarily turning away with the essence of viewing things as "self" and "mine," there is still a mere turning away, the text shows: *from seeing impurity and so forth*. The phrase: *in the nature of hatred* is used because it thoroughly connects to a single object of hatred. 

Furthermore, the answer to the upcoming explanation—*Because love and so forth do not contradict delusion, they do not utterly destroy faults*—is shown by the phrase: *by meditating on the unattractive* <note>original: "asubhabhāvanā", a meditation technique used to counter attachment by visualizing the decaying stages of a corpse</note>. 

In response to the question, "Why does it not also become a view of impermanence and so forth?" the text says: *if there is a self*. To show the contradiction between the error of viewing things as impermanent and the truth, the phrase: *when it depends on causes* is used. 

Because those who are free from desire lack the view of a self, hatred—which has the view of a self as its essence—is impossible for them. Therefore, to show that those individuals are possessed of hatred and not compassion <note>This follows the opponent's logical premise for refutation</note>, the text says: *delusion is the root of faults*. *To the cause of faults* refers to that which causes harm. *Faultless* means not being possessed of faults. <summary>This page analyzes the logical relationship between the egoic view of "self" and "mine" and the arising of hatred, arguing that true compassion requires moving beyond conceptual constructions of selfhood. It uses the "king" analogy to explain how enlightened beings act for others' benefit based on previous momentum even without egoic striving.</summary>

དང་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་དང་ཉེ་བར་གཞལ་བ་རྣམས་ལ་ནི་འདིར་དགག་པ་བརྗོད་པར་མི་བྱ་སྟེ། གང་གི་ཕྱིར། གང་དུ་ཕྱིར། གང་དུ་རྗེས་དཔག་ལ་སོགས་འདི། །བཀག་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དེ་ཡང་བཀག །འདིར་རང་གི་འདོད་པ་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་བསྒྲུབས་པ་མེད་དོ#། །
འབྲེལ་བ་གཞན་མ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །འདིར་ཅུང་ཟད་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་བྱེ་བྲག་པའི་འདོད་པ་ཁ་ཅིག་ལས་སོ། །དེས་ན་དེ་བཀག་པ་བཞིན་དུ་འདི་ཡང་#བཀག་པར་རིག་#པར་བྱའོ། །དོན་གྱི་གོ་བ་གཉིས་ཀ་ལ་འགག་པར་#བརྗོད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དོན་གོ་རྣམས་ནི་#མཐའ་གཅིག་ཏུ#། །ངེས་པ་དང་མཐའ་
གཅིག་ཏུ་མ་ངེས་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་གང་མཐའ་གཅིག་ཏུ་ངེས་ཏེ། རྗེས་དཔག་གང་དུ་མཐའ་གཅིག་ཏུ་ངེས་པ་ཅན་གྱི་#གོ་བ་ནི་དཔེར་ན་དེ་འཚོད་པ་ལས་སྣོད་དང་རྟེན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དོན་འཛིན་པ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་འཚོད་པའི་རྟགས་ཉིད་ལས་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྗེས་སུ་དཔག་པ་ལས་ཐ་དད་པ་མ་

Regarding instruction, subsequent instruction, and comparison, we shall not express a refutation here. Why is this?

Because, just as <term>inference</term> <gloss>anumāna</gloss> and the others have been refuted elsewhere, they are refuted in the same way here. In this context, we have not established even a small portion of our own preferred systems of inference and so forth.

This is because no other connection has been shown. The brief discussion provided here concerns certain assertions of the <term>Vaisheshika</term> <gloss>a school of Indian philosophy emphasizing atomism and categories</gloss>. Therefore, you should understand that just as their assertions were refuted, this is also refuted.

We shall discuss the refutation regarding both types of <term>implication</term> <gloss>arthāpatti</gloss>. Implicit meanings are of two kinds:
The certain and the uncertain.

Regarding the certain: wherever there is an implication characterized by certainty, it is like perceiving the purpose of a vessel or a support from the act of cooking. Because this is understood from the very sign of cooking, it is not distinct from inference.

The other type <insert>is false</insert>. That which is characterized as uncertain implication is not a valid means of cognition at all, because it is a cause for doubt. For example, when it is said that something is impermanent because it is produced by effort, it is uncertain to say it is permanent because it is not produced by effort.

Regarding the statement that the indication of Nagpa being outside because he is not in the house constitutes the valid cognition of <term>non-existence</term> <gloss>abhāva</gloss>:
The absence of Nagpa in the house
Does not indicate that he is outside.
From the meaning of the word house here,
One thoroughly understands he is outside.

In the phrase "Nagpa is not in the house," the understanding that Nagpa is outside is realized through the implication of the usage of the word "house" itself, not from the non-existence. If he were absent from both the house and the outside, one would simply say, "He does not exist." Therefore, this implication of an external object is not a separate valid cognition of non-existence.

From the failure to establish the opposing side,
The own-position is said to be established.
This refers to when the <term>Samkhya</term> <gloss>one of the oldest schools of Indian philosophy, dualistic in nature</gloss> practitioners wish to establish their own position by refuting the position of others. You should understand that this method of removing consequences is also being dismissed.

The definitive explanation of inference for oneself is completed.

<summary>This page critiques various Indian philosophical systems of logic, specifically refuting the Vaisheshika and Samkhya schools while arguing that implication and non-existence are not independent means of valid cognition but are contained within inference.</summary>
<keywords>inference, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, implication, non-existence, valid cognition, logic, Nagpa</keywords>

ཐ་དད་མེད་ཕྱིར་ཀུན་དུ་མཐོང་། ༈ །དེ་ཡང་གསལ་#བ་ལ་ལྟོས་མིན། །གསལ་བྱེད་རྟོགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན། །གསལ་བྱ་ཡང་དག་རྟོགས་པ་མིན། །སྤྱི་དང་དེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དག །ཅི་ཡི་ཕྱིར་ན་བཟློག་པར་འདོད། ༈ །ཐ་དད་མེད་དོན་མེད་པར་ཡང་། །འཚེད་པ་པོ་སོགས་བརྗོད་པ་

མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །རྒྱུ་མཚན་ཅན་མིན་ཐོབ་ཕྱིར་རོ། ༈ །རྗེས་འགྲོ་མེད་ཕྱིར་ནུས་པའང་མིན། །གལ་ཏེ་འཚེད་#པོ་ཉིད་སོགས་སྤྱི#། །དང་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་དེ་ཡོད་སོགས། །བཞིན་དུ་གསལ་འགྱུར་མིན་ན་ནི། །ཁྱད་པར་མེད་ཕྱིར་ཕྱིས་མི་འགྱུར། ༈ །བྱ་བས་ཕན་འདོགས་ལྟོས་གསལ་བྱེད། །

དངོས་པོའི་རྗེས་འགྲོ་གཞན་མེད་ན། །གཅིག་གི་#འབྲས་བུ་གཞན་གྱིར་མིན#། །ཤིན་ཏུ་ཐ་དད་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། ༈ །གལ་ཏེ་བདག་ཉིད་གཅིག་པ་ཡིས། །དུ་མ་འབྲས་བུ་གཅིག་བྱེད་ན། །བདག་ཉིད་གཅིག་ལའང་དེ་ཡོད་ཕྱིར། །ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པ་དོན་མེད་འགྱུར། །ཐ་དད་མེད་པའི་ངོ་

If it is not different, there is no "following after."
If it is different, it is not the support. 
It does not go there, nor does it exist there.
It does not possess parts that exist later.
It does not abandon its previous support.
Alas, this is indeed the cause of misfortune! 
That which has come to abide in another,
Does not move from its own place;
And if it abides in a new location that has arisen,
That would be extremely reasonable. 
In the place where that entity abides,
There is no connection;
And yet it pervades those objects—
Is that not a great wonder? 
If the class existed everywhere,
Then by manifesting in one, it would be manifested;
Because there is no difference, it would be seen everywhere. 
That too does not depend on the manifestation.
If the manifester is not perceived,
The "to be manifested" is not correctly perceived.
The universal and that which possesses it—
Why do you wish to reverse them? 
Even without a non-different object,
One says "the cook" and so forth. 
Because they are distinct, the action is not the cause. 
Because it is not this class, and is connected to the action. 
Because hearing is caused by another,
The action too does not have an abiding state. 
Because there is no connection, it is not that the universal
Is not unreasonable as the cause of the word.
Because of over-extension, even if there were no action,
It would not be for cognition or expression,
Because it would follow that it is not based on a reason. 
Because there is no "following after," there is no capacity.
If the "being a cook" and so forth were a universal,
If it does not manifest at the very first
Like "existence" and so forth,
It will not do so later, as there is no difference. 
If it is a manifester depending on the benefit of the action,
Then being unchanging, there is no dependence.
Even if this excellence exists,
Because of momentariness, from what action? 
If the distinct are similar, then the class—
By whatever proximity it engages in some
And not in others—that itself
Is the cause of the word and the cognition. 
If there is no other "following after" of the entity
That is free from exclusion,
"The result of one is not that of another,
Because they are completely distinct," if you say that: 
If, by being a single essence,
The many produce a single result,
Because that exists in even a single essence,
The "cooperating cause" would be meaningless.

རུང་བ་དེ་ཉིད་#ལ་ཡང་ཐེ་ཚོམ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་དེ། ལྐོག་ཤལ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གྲུབ་ན་བ་ལང་གི་#ཐ་སྙད་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཡུལ་ཡོད་ན་ཡང་རྨོངས་པས་འདིར། །གཞན་དག་རྗེས་སུ་མི་བརྗོད་པ། །གྲུབ་པ་དང་ནི་ཆོས་མཐུན་པས། །བརྡ་བསྟན་བྱེད་པ་#འབའ་ཞིག་གོ། །ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་དང་མ་མཐོང་
ལས། །རྒྱུ་དང་འབྲས་#ཉིད་སྒྲུབ་པ་བཞིན། །དེ་གཉིས་ལ་ནི་འབྲས་སོགས་སྒྲ། །ཐ་སྙད་དོན་དུ་བཀོད་པ་ཡིན། །རྒྱུ་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་རབ་བསྒྲུབ་#པ། །འདི་ནི་རང་བཞིན་ནང་འདུས་ཕྱིར། །གཏན་ཚིགས་རབ་དབྱེ་བཤད་པ་ལས། །ཐ་དད་པར་ནི་དཔེར་མ་བརྗོད། །ཅེས་བྱ་བ་

There is absolutely nothing else. This is because this has been experienced previously not just once. There is no need to establish a connection between these. Therefore, if the <term>non-perception of the perceptible</term> <gloss>the fact that something which should be visible is not seen</gloss> is established, there is no doubt regarding the cognition and the words characterized by its absence. It is like the <term>conventional designation</term> <gloss>naming or labeling</gloss> of an ox when the dewlap and other features are established.

->Even if the object exists, through delusion<-
->Others are not described here;<-
->Because of the similarity with what is established,<-
->It is merely a demonstration of the <term>convention</term> <gloss>agreed-upon symbolic usage</gloss>.<--

->Just as from seeing and not seeing<-
->Causes and effects are established,<-
->In both cases, the words "effect" and so on<-
->Are applied for the sake of convention.<-

->Establishing the effect from the cause<-
->Is included within the <term>essential nature</term> <gloss>the identity or natural relation</gloss>;<-
->Because it was explained in the "Classification of Reasons,"<-
->It was not cited as a separate example.<-

These are the intermediate verses. From <term>non-perception</term> <gloss>the absence of observing a qualified object</gloss>, one establishes the suitability of the conventional usage of the "non-existence" of an essential nature that would differentiate it. The <term>pervasion</term> <gloss>the necessary logical connection</gloss> is also established elsewhere from the mere convention, because there is no distinction. It has already been explained that because the non-existence that is the identity of non-perception is established, the convention of non-existence is established.

If one asks: How is that non-perception itself established as non-existent, and how does it occur in someone's continuum? That fault does not exist because:

->From the experience of perceiving one thing,<-
->The conceptual mind will arise<-
->Thinking "this is perceived"<-
->Or "this is not perceived."<-

It is not the case that "this is not perceived" arises merely through the absence of the specific cognition of things from which the convention of non-existence would arise. Then what is it? It arises from the presence of a cognition that is distinct from itself; for if everything were not perceived in some way, one would not realize the non-existence of a thing. ཕྱིར་གཏན་ཚིགས་མ་བསྟན་ནའང་། །དེ་ནི་ཡོད་པར་དོགས་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །དངོས་པོ་འགལ་བ་དག་ལ་ཡང་། །ཁྱབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་མཐོང་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་གཏན་ཚིགས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་མི་མཐུན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་མེད་པར་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་ན། བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ལོག་པ་ལ་གཏན་
ཚིགས་ལྡོག་པས་ཁྱབ་པར་འགྱུར་ན། དེ་ལ་དེ་མེད་པ་ལ་ཚད་མ་ཡང་མ་མཐོང་ངོ་། །མི་#འགལ་བ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ལ་ཡང་དགག་པ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་རིགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐལ་ཆེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཐ་དད་པའི་འགལ་བ་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་འབྱུང་བ་ཅན་དག་ཀྱང་མཐོང་བའི་ཕྱིར། གཅིག་
ལ་མཐོང་བ་ཡང་གཞན་ལ་མེད་པ་ཉིད་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བརྩལ་མ་ཐག་ཏུ་འབྱུང་བ་ཉིད་དང་ཅིག་ཤོས་དག་ལ་མི་རྟག་པ་ཉིད་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་རྣམ་པ་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། མེད་པ་ཉིད་ཁོ་ན་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདི་ལྟར། ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ནི་མི་དམིགས་ཕྱིར། མེད་ཉིད་མི་འགྲུབ་ཅེས་ནི་བཤད། །མེད་
པ་ཉིད་ནི་མི་འགྲུབ་ན། །ལྡོག་པ་ཉིད་ལ་ཐེ་ཚོམ་ཟ། །སྐྱེས་བུ་ཙམ་འདིས་ནི་ཐམས་ཅད་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན་གང་གིས་ན་འདིའི་མཐོང་བ་ལྡོག་པས་དེ་ལྟར་མི་འགྱུར། གང་གི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཤེས་བྱ་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་ལ་འཁྲུལ་པ་མེད་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གཟིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མེད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་

Regardless of the case, if one asks whether this <note>the creator or a causal factor</note> acts as the cause here, consider the following. If a collection of conditions such as karma <note>intentional action</note> exists, and previously the effect was not perceived, but then it is perceived because of the presence of that collection of conditions, then such a causal change would occur. However, it is not possible for it to have that capacity because a collection of conditions cannot be perceived in its entirety by its own nature. To show that Ishvara <note>the Lord or Creator God</note> is also not a logical cause, the Commentary <note>referring to Dharmakirti's Pramanavarttika</note> provides another formulation by saying: "Or rather." For this reason, following this explanation, a second syllogism is constructed.

If one asks how he <note>Ishvara</note> could not be the cause if he engages in creating the world after thinking about it, the text says: "From all things such as attachment and so forth." The phrase "the world" and what follows refers to the doubts of others. The response begins with "It is not an answer." Because he is subject to the influence of the karma of others in the other world, he is not Ishvara <note>the Lord/Independent One</note> at all; he is entirely dependent. Therefore, how could what was described be Ishvara? He is simply not a lord. 

If it is argued that the specific characteristic of being under the influence of another's karma was done out of compassion for that world, the reply is: "Because of the establishment of hells and so forth," meaning animals and <term>preta</term> <gloss>hungry ghosts</gloss>. Because he created these, he is without compassion. How could he be a lord? It is illogical for one possessing compassion to act in such a way. The intent is: why does he not create only happiness for everyone? 

Others mention "the karma of the world itself." If one says that because he creates suffering such as hell, those in hell and elsewhere suffer, but Ishvara lacks the power to make beings happy, the refutation is: "This is not supreme." If that were the case, then Ishvara would not be supreme at all. If you ask why, the text says: "If he were supreme," and so forth. "Even if he lacks the power" means being devoid of capacity. <summary>This page critiques the concept of a creator god or Ishvara by arguing that dependence on karma and the existence of suffering in hells contradict the attributes of independence and compassion. The text uses logical syllogisms to demonstrate that a truly supreme being would not produce a world filled with misery.</summary>

འཇིགས་པས་ན་བར་དང་བཅས་པ་ཉིད་ཁས་ལེན་པའོ། །ལན་དུ་དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་བར་གྱི་ཤ་ལྷག་དང་འདྲ་བ་ལྡན་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བརྟགས་པས་ཅི་ཞིག་བྱ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་དགོངས་པའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་ཡན་ལག་ཅན་མེད་ཅིང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རེག་པ་མ་ཡིན་ན། དེའི་ཚེ་རྡུལ་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ་བཞིན་
དུ་བརྡེགས་ན། སོ་སོར་ཅི་སྟེ་མི་དགྱེས་ཤིང་བར་དུ་བཅས་པས་སྒྲིབ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྐྱེད་པ་དང་། གསེང་དང་བཅས་པར་ཆུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འཛིན་པར་ཡང་ཅི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་ན། གང་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ་ཚོགས་པ་གང་ལའོ། །སོ་སོར་དགྱེས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ནི་སིལ་བུར་འཐོར་བའོ། །དེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་
ནི་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་བརྩད་པའོ། །རྡུལ་རྣམས་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཐོང་བ་དང་། མ་མཐོང་བ་དང་། མ་མཐོང་བའི་ཚོགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཡང་ན་པ་རའི་སྒྲ་ནི་འབའ་ཞིག་གི་དོན་ཡིན་པར་རྡུལ་རྣམས་ཚོགས་པ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཡིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་
ཏེ། ཡན་ལག་ཅན་གྱི་རྫས་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལ་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་དཔེར་ན་སྒྲ་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །འབྲས་བུ་གཞན་ཡང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྒྲིབ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །དེར་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གཞན་གྱིའོ། །སྒྲ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བར་དང་བཅས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་རྣམ་པ་གཅིག་ཏུ་རྟོགས་པ་འདིར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་
བར་ནི་ཡུལ་དེར་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་གནོད་བྱེད་སྐྱེས་པས་འཇོག་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་སྐབས་ལ་ནི་དེ་ལྟར་གནོད་བྱེད་ཡོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་བསམས་པའོ། །ལན་དུ་འདི་ལ་ཡང་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་ཞེས་མ་ངེས་པའི་དོན་གྱིས་གནོད་པའམ། སྒྲུབ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདི་སྔ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེ་ན། བདེན་ཏེ་འདིས་ནི་སྲིད་པར་

<meta>This page continues a complex debate on the nature of physical composition and contact within the Pramana (Logic and Epistemology) section of the Tengyur. It specifically addresses the relationship between atoms, parts, and the whole.</meta>

The meaning is as follows. Anticipating the doubt that there is contact <note>original: "reg go"</note>, the text states, "and contact as well." Why is this? Because that <note>contact</note> does not exist, for there are no individual sides <note>atoms being indivisible and thus lacking distinct faces to touch</note>. The term "conjunction" <note>original: "ldan pa"</note> belongs to the opponent's position. It is argued that things with intervals between them produce conjunction, and thereby produce a "composite whole" <note>original: "yan lag can", literally "that which possesses parts"</note>. 

In response, the text says "that itself." The reason for raising the point "if they touch" is the desire to point out another fault. Addressing that, it says "another conjunction," meaning that because there are no gaps, things like protection and covering are established. 

The phrase "nevertheless" <note>original: "on te"</note> refers to the fear that if the produced effect is meaningless, it will be refuted; therefore, the opponent accepts that there are intervals. In response, it says "if that is the case." The intention is to ask: if that is so, what is the use of analyzing conjunctions and such, which are like excess flesh in the gaps?

If there is no composite whole and the atoms do not touch, then when a mass of atoms is struck, why do they not scatter individually? Furthermore, how could things with intervals create obstructions or hold water and other liquids if they are porous? To address this, the text says "in which," meaning in whichever collection. To "scatter individually" means to break apart into fragments. 

The word "that" refers to what you have disputed. The statement "atoms are the supreme collection" means that through the power of visible, invisible, and partially visible collections, they are seen as "supreme" or "distinguished." Alternatively, the word "para" <note>Sanskrit for "supreme" or "other"</note> means "only," implying that atoms are only a collection and not a substantial composite whole.

Regarding the second point, it says "for example, sound." "Other effects" refers to things like obstruction. The word "there" refers to the other's position. Regarding the idea that sound and other things with intervals are perceived as a single type, it is thought that since a hindrance arises when reaching that location, it is established; however, in this context, no such hindrance exists. In response, it says "to this also." If you say that this proof or refutation is previously non-existent due to an uncertain meaning, that is true, for through this, in existence...

<summary>This page critiques the concept of a "composite whole" by analyzing whether atoms truly touch or maintain intervals. It argues that physical properties like obstruction and cohesion are results of atomic collections rather than a separate overarching substance.</summary>
<keywords>atoms, composite whole, conjunction, Pramana, epistemology, physical composition, contact, collection</keywords>

བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དེ་དག་ནི་དམན་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི་དེའི་ཞིང་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །བརྩེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བློ་དེས་ཞིང་དུ་བྱས་པའི་རྒྱུ་གང་ལ་ཡོད་པ་ཞེས་ཚིག་རྣམ་པར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་ནི་ཆུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་མ་ཡིན་པས་ནའོ། །དེ་དག་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་
བརྩེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །རྒྱས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཞན་པར་ལྟ་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། ཡང་ནས་ཡང་དུ་རྒྱས་པ་ཁོ་ནར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །དེ་ཡང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཆོང་བ་ཡང་ངོ་། །དེའི་ཆོས་ནི་མངོན་པར་འཕེལ་བ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་མེད་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཡང་མ་
ཡིན་ཏེ། །དེས་བཟློག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། སྐབས་ཀྱི་ཤེས་རབ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལ་འཕེལ་བ་མཐར་ཐུག་པ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་སེམས་ནའོ། །སྟོབས་དང་རྩོལ་བ་དག་ལས་མཆོང་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་འབྲེལ་ཏོ། །མཆོང་བ་སྟོབས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་དོན་དུ་ལྡོག་

Is it not observed that people engage in actions because they see a benefit? Why then is it expressed in that way? To this, the text says: in return for compassion <insert>etc.</insert>. The compassion and other qualities of a Bodhisattva <note>an awakened being who acts for the benefit of others</note> do not depend on receiving a benefit in return. Instead, they arise from a mind of a similar type, such as wisdom and the like.

For that very reason, it is said that these qualities are not inferior, using the phrase: in that field. One should apply the phrase to mean: whoever possesses the cause that has been made into a field by that mind of compassion and so on. Therefore, it is said that they do not become small or diminished. Regarding the term "those," it refers to compassion and the rest. Since they possess the characteristic of not failing to increase, how could they ever be seen as weak? The meaning is that they will simply grow further and further.

Regarding the phrase "that too," it refers to "leaping" <note>likely referring to a sudden or vast advancement in spiritual capacity</note>. Its quality is one of an increase that has no ultimate limit. However, that is not the case; it is reversed by that. One might think that the wisdom and other qualities of this specific context do not have a limitless increase. The text connects this by saying that leaping arises from strength and effort.

To explain the reversal in order to accomplish the result of leaping, strength, and so on, it says: even for one who has practiced the best leaping very well. The intent is to show that these two are the causes of leaping.

One might ask: if that is so, and if the leaping were to become limitless, would those two <note>strength and effort</note> not become something that does not remain stable? To this, the text says: strength and... The nature of remaining stable is the very persistence of capacity. To speak of a stable nature means to be individually certain. Otherwise, it is not so, meaning it would not be limitless.

This arises from the very nature of habituation <gloss>familiarization or repetitive practice</gloss>, not merely from strength and effort. Thus, the thought is that these two alone are not the actual continuum of that leaping. If it were not so, meaning if it were not the result of habituation, then it would follow that it could not be established later. This should be understood by the phrase: even before. Why is that? Because its cause...

<summary>This page discusses the nature of a Bodhisattva's compassion and wisdom, arguing that these qualities arise from habituation rather than a desire for reward. It explores the mechanics of spiritual progress, specifically how repetitive practice leads to limitless growth beyond mere physical effort.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, compassion, wisdom, habituation, leaping, spiritual progress, cause and effect</keywords>

The desire to attain pleasure and to avoid suffering is precisely what the <term>Sutras</term> <gloss>scriptures containing the Buddha's discourses</gloss> categorize as the craving for existence and the craving for annihilation. When it is said that these are "precisely those desires for existence and destruction," one might wonder: how can these be considered the desire for existence? In response, the text states, "that which is this..." and so forth. By the word "etcetera," we should include the possession of pleasure and the separation from suffering.

The meaning is as follows: the term "existence" <term>bhava</term> serves as a synonym for cyclic existence <term>samsara</term>. This encompasses cyclic existence itself, the environment, necessary resources, the possession of happiness, and the separation from suffering. Regarding these, it is said that three types of desire arise. This desire for existence applies to all of them; it is not limited to just one. The classification of this very desire begins with the phrase "of desire" and so forth. To specifically demonstrate this classification, the text says "that which..." and so forth. By the word "etcetera," the necessary resources are understood. When there is no contradiction, that term is used.

The explanation of the Noble Truth of the Origin <note>original: "samudaya-satya," the second of the Four Noble Truths describing the cause of suffering</note> is found in the phrase "desire for existence." Therefore, all three of these cravings constitute the Truth of the Origin. The thematic point is that they are established as three types of paths according to the distinctions in how they function.

To prove through another method that craving itself is the cause of rebirth, the text states, "attachment to a self." The phrase "to all" refers to the environment, necessary resources, and so on. The cause that leads to the perception of pleasure in what is actually not pleasure is precisely this attachment to a self, and nothing else. Because it is the cause of this engagement, existence itself is the support for craving.

If one wonders how this teaching can be valid since there is no self <term>anatman</term>, the text says, "of the ego-grasping." That which possesses the alternative name of "attachment" or "craving" is the cause; it acts as a contributing factor. If one questions how it serves as a cause, the text explains by following the root verse: "that which engages thoroughly with all..."

<summary>This page discusses the classification of craving within the framework of the Four Noble Truths, specifically identifying how attachment to a self drives the desire for existence and pleasure. It explains that the Truth of the Origin consists of three types of craving that support the cycle of rebirth.</summary>

<keywords>craving, existence, annihilation, Noble Truth of the Origin, samsara, attachment to self, ego-grasping, Buddhist logic</keywords>

བྱ་བ་ནི་མི་རྟག་པ་ཙམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཁོ་ནས་སོ། །དེས་ན་རྣམ་པ་དེ་འདྲ་བའི་སྤྱིའོ། །འོ་ན་གང་གི་ཚེ་ཉེས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེ་ན། མི་རྟག་པ་ཙམ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཉིད་དུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འབའ་ཞིག་པའི་ཆོས་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་སོ། །གཅིག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཅན་ལ་གཉིས་པ་མི་རྟག་པ་ཉིད་བསྒྲུབས་ན་ཕན་
ཚུན་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཚོགས་པ་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་གཅིག་ལ་གཉིས་པ་བསྒྲུབས་པས་ཚོགས་པར་འགྲུབ་ན་འོ་ན་ཅི་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ཚོགས་པ་བཟློག་པ་འབའ་ཞིག་འགལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཞིག་ན་དེ་ལས་གཞན་བཟློག་པ་ཡང་ཡིན་ཏེ་དེས་ན་སྒྲའི་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱི་མི་རྟག་པ་ཉིད་ལ་

If the pervasive adherence were to apply to things that are not burning and so forth, then it would be deceptive. However, when one adheres to the burning quality of fire and smoke, and their capacity to burn is just as it appears, then it is not deceptive. What is the certainty of this? There is no certainty at all that such adherence is restricted only to the functional capacity of an object and not to anything else; this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "cause and effect": the adherence to the pervasion between fire and smoke is indirectly preceded by the actual fire and smoke. Therefore, there is certainty regarding those two. How is this certainty grasped? It is grasped as the effect of the adherence to the pervasion between fire and smoke. Regarding the phrase "convention" <term>vyavahāra</term> <gloss>social or linguistic usage</gloss>: it arises from the very convention of designating the certainty of pervasion regarding fire and smoke.

This is stated because the desired point is expressed as the <term>sādhya</term> <gloss>the thing to be proven</gloss>. Regarding the phrase "the opposite of that": it is to establish the opposite of what was reduced to an absurdity. If one wonders how, the text says: "How is this the <term>heṭu</term> <gloss>logical reason</gloss>?"

Whatever impermanence is distinguished by something other than the <term>dharmin</term> <gloss>the subject of the quality</gloss>, it establishes that non-existence also, because it is understood through the pervasion of the opposite. Regarding the term "impermanence": that which possesses the sound of impermanence is the nature of the thing; in that way, it is not establishing the sound itself. It is "in such a manner" because it establishes merely the impermanence. Therefore, it is a generality of that kind.

If you ask: "When does it become a fault?" It is when there is "mere impermanence." It is "in such a manner" because it establishes the quality in isolation. བྱ་བའོ། །གང་གི་ཕྱིར་འདི་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་ངེས་པའི་ངག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བརྗོད་པ་ཅན་ཡིན་པ་དེས་ན། རང་གི་ཚིག་དང་བསྟན་བཅོས་ཚད་མ་ཡིན་པར་གཅིག་ཏུ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིད་ཆེས་པ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་སློབ་དཔོན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གླང་པོས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །གཉི་ག་ཡང་ཁས་བླངས་པའི་ཚད་

དག་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་མཚུངས་པ་ཉིད་སྟོན་པ་ནི། ཅི་ལྟར་བདག་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །དེར་བསྟེན་མིན་ན་སྟེ་བསྟན་བཅོས་ཁས་མ་བླངས་པར་རོ། །དེས་ཅི་ཞིག་བརྗོད་སྙམ་ན། ཅི་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །སྨྲ་བ་ཀུན་ནི་{བརྫུན་,རྫུན་}ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེ་ནི་འགོག་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་

This is the perspective of the earlier <term>scholars</term>. The phrase self and others does not mean that this is stated to be harmful; rather, it identifies the specific object that is accepted as being harmful. The term desired means accepted with conviction. If one asks how, it is the phrase possessing perfect certainty. Because this contains a statement possessing speech that determines the perfect meaning, the <term>Acarya</term> <gloss>Master</gloss> Dignaga explained it this way: to be convinced that one's own words and the <term>shastras</term> <gloss>treatises</gloss> are uniquely authoritative. This is because both are equally valid as accepted authorities.

If one then asks whether certainty arises from inference, the text says because of the confusion of conventional terms. The phrase together with refers to that very conviction. If one does not accept one's own words and the treatises as authoritative, then those statements and the investigation into that teaching would not exist. To show this equality, the text says just as I am. If one does not rely on them, it means not accepting the treatises. If one wonders what that implies, it asks how? The statement all speech is false is not a negation. Why? Because if the statement all speech is false were itself a negation, <note>then the statement itself would be false, leading to a logical contradiction similar to the Liar Paradox.</note>

If one wonders how this is refuted, the text says in this way. If one wonders where this comes from, the word speech is mentioned. If everything existing in the three times <note>past, present, and future</note> were not authoritative, then what would be the point of stating them? If one states them and then says they are not authoritative, the text uses the example after washing. 

<note>The author provides a humorous analogy for logical inconsistency.</note>
When someone is asked, "What are you doing?" while they are picking up a <term>laddu</term> <gloss>sweetmeat</gloss> that has fallen into manure, and they reply, "I will wash it and then throw it away," it is just like that. To first state a proposition existing in the three times as authoritative, and then later discard that speech by claiming it is not authoritative, is the same process. 

To anticipate an objection: if one says that it is established as non-authoritative because of later regret, the answer is even if that were the case. If one asks how it is contradictory, the text says the state of not having spoken. The act refers to the speech itself. This very point is the state of not having been investigated. Why?

<summary>This page discusses the logical necessity of accepting the authority of one's own words and treatises in formal debate. It uses the famous paradox of 'all speech is false' and a colorful analogy of washing a sweet fallen in manure to illustrate the absurdity of making a claim only to immediately invalidate its authority.</summary>
<keywords>Dignaga, authority, pramana, shastra, logical contradiction, speech, three times, debate theory</keywords>

<meta>The text belongs to the Pramana (Logic and Epistemology) section of the Tengyur, specifically focusing on the mechanisms of inference and the validity of perception regarding others' mental states.</meta>

...manifestation. <note>The text continues a technical analysis of how an object or thought is made present to the mind.</note>

The phrase "by that" refers to inference <term>anumāna</term> <gloss>logical deduction from a sign</gloss>.

The statement that "there is no certainty of truthful speech because the object is uncertain" is expressed by the phrase "by another."

The phrase "in that way" means being understood by another person.

The phrase "that itself" refers to whatever is understood by another.

The phrase "therefore" indicates that because there is no certainty in the truthfulness of the speech itself, there is no understanding of the actual thing through another person’s understanding.

If one were to understand that, it would lead to the fault of mutual dependence <note>original: "anyonyāśraya," a logical fallacy where two propositions rely on each other for proof</note>.

How so? The phrase "mutual" is used because if one describes the understanding of one person in terms of the other, that constitutes the understanding, and because that understanding is also what describes the other.

The phrase "but if" refers to any transformation such as a brightening of the face. This is produced by an object that has become manifest to me, just as, for example, the transformation of my own face brightening occurs. This refers to the idea that "the transformation of this person’s face brightening is also a transformation of a brightening face."

The expression of "that itself" refers to "the transformation of such a nature." By seeing such a transformation, like a brightening of the face, that other perceiver also understands exactly what I have seen.

The response to this is "then that very nature," which means it is of a similar type. That is an inference.

If you ask why this is not logical, it is because of the phrase "inference is..."

If you ask why, the example of "smoke" is used. It is that which is seen in the example itself. However, what is established is something of a similar type to what was seen in the example.

Similarly, here too, from the transformation of a brightening face residing in a tree <note>This likely refers to a spirit or being associated with a tree, or a metaphorical placeholder in a logical syllogism</note>, one establishes a similar type to the certain cause, but they are not the same identical object.

To express another refutation, the phrase "if" is used. It should be connected to "why is the self not also one?" Any transformation such as a brightening of the face is my truth or is made by me, just as, for example, the transformation of my own face brightening occurs. The transformation of this person’s face and so on is also a transformation of a brightening face...

<summary>This page discusses the logical fallacies of mutual dependence in the context of inference and perception. It uses the physical sign of a brightening face as a case study to distinguish between identical objects and similar types of phenomena in epistemic proof.</summary>
<keywords>inference, mutual dependence, perception, Pramana, logical sign, epistemology, Tengyur</keywords>

པ་གོ་ཅི་ལྟར་མི་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། འདི་ལྟར་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །ཅི་མ་དམིགས་སྙམ་ན། དྲན་པ་ལ་མངོན་དུ་གནས་པའི་དགག་པར་བྱ་བ་འདི་ནིའོ། །ས་ཕྱོགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དབེན་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་ཉམས་སུ་མྱོང་བ་ཉིད་གཞན་མ་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཤེས་པ་གཏན་མེད་པ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འོ་
ན་དེའི་བདག་ཉིད་འགོག་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་ཅི་ལྟར་གཞན་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། གང་གི་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །འདི་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མྱོང་བཞིན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །གཞན་གྱི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དྲན་པ་ལ་གནས་པའི་བུམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུའོ། །རང་བཞིན་དེས་དེ་ལྟར་
མ་དམིགས་ཀྱང་ཅི་ལྟར་དེས་དབེན་པ་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། གཅིག་དམིགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་འདིར་རོ། །གང་ཞེ་ན། དེའི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་སྟེ་བུམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའིའོ། །འདི་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ས་ཕྱོགས་སོ། །ས་ཕྱོགས་བུམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བདག་ཉིད་དུ་མ་དམིགས་པ་ཉིད་དོ་བུམ་པ་ལ་
སོགས་པའི་དབེན་པ་ཉིད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །གཞན་གྱི་བསམ་པས་ལྡོག་པ་མེད་པར་དོགས་པ་བསུ་བ་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །བུམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་དེས་ཕྱོགས་འདི་ན་མེད་པའོ་ཞེས་དེ་ལྟར་བུམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་མེད་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའོ། །བཟློག་
སྟེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ལས་བཟློག་པ་སྟེ། ས་ཕྱོགས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་ལ་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པའི་སྒྲས་བརྗོད། ཅི་ལྟར་ས་ཕྱོགས་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉིད་དུ་བུམ་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་མེད་པར་བསྒྲུབ་སྟེ་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པར་གཞན་ཉིད་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དོན་ཏོ། །
ལན་ནི་འདི་ནི་ཞིག་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །གང་གི་ཚེ་ཞེ་ན་གལ་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའོ། །འདིའི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། ས་ཕྱོགས་བུམ་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་བརྗོད་པའིའོ། །གལ་ཏེ་ས་ཕྱོགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དོན་དངོས་པོའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་གཞན་ནང་དུ་མི་འདུ་བ་ཡིན་ནའོ། །ནང་

If there is no such thing as an entity with the nature of emptiness, then how is it that we point to something distinct by saying, "there is no flask on this patch of ground"? To address this, the text says: "For that reason." The phrase "in that way" refers to the distinction. Pointing out the specific form is what is meant by the word "flask."

If it is true that there is no separate "voidness" apart from the object, one might ask: "Since that object is perceived, how can it be a case of non-perception?" To this, the text says: "In this way." If you wonder what is not perceived, it is this: the object of negation which remains present in the memory. The term "patch of ground" refers to the actual experience of a vacant patch of ground, which constitutes the non-perception of another object; it does not mean there is a total absence of cognition.

One might then ask: "In the context of negating the essence of that object, how is it that something else is perceived?" The text says: "Because of which." The phrase "this" refers to the ground or similar area currently being experienced. The phrase "of the other" refers to the nature of the flask or similar object present in the memory.

One might further ask: "Even if it is not perceived as having that nature, how is it void of that nature?" The text addresses this with: "perceiving one," and so on. If you ask "of what?", the text says "of that," meaning of the flask or similar object. The word "this" refers to the patch of ground. The meaning is that the patch of ground itself, not being perceived as having the essence of a flask or similar object, constitutes the "voidness" of the flask.

To anticipate the objection that there might be no exclusion of the other's intended meaning, the text says: "If." The fact that the entity—the flask or similar object—is not in this location is how we establish the absence of the flask. The phrase "in reverse" means the opposite of a non-entity. One applies the term "non-entity" to the existing patch of ground. The meaning is: "How can one establish that the patch of ground itself lacks the nature of a flask, and thus establish that the 'other' is a non-entity?"

The response is: "In this case, when..." If you ask "when?", the text says: "If." The word "of this" refers to the statement "the patch of ground does not have the nature of a flask." This applies if the object, such as the patch of ground, which exists as a real entity, does not include the other within it.

<summary>This page discusses the Buddhist logic of negation and emptiness, explaining that the absence of an object like a flask is not a separate "thing" but rather the perception of a vacant space where the object is remembered but not found. It clarifies that "non-entity" refers to a specific relationship between an existing location and a missing object.</summary>
<keywords>negation, non-perception, emptiness, flask, patch of ground, entity, logic, Buddhist epistemology</keywords>
